sources.title: The Apollo Experiment That Keeps on Giving

facts.claim: NASA identifies Eagle as LM-5 and Columbia as CSM-107.
NASA lists an LM-5 integrated systems test on November 21, 1968.
NASA lists an LM-5 acceptance test on December 13, 1968.
The ascent stage was delivered to Kennedy on January 8, 1969; the descent stage followed on January 12.
facts.evidenceExcerpt:
1/8/69 – LM-5 ascent stage delivered to Kennedy
1/12/69 – LM-5 descent stage delivered to Kennedy

facts.claim: Apollo 11 launched on July 16, 1969 at 9:32 a.m. EDT from Launch Pad 39A on Saturn-V AS-506.
facts.evidenceExcerpt:
July 16, 1969; 9:32 a.m. EDT
Launch Pad 39A
Saturn-V AS-506

facts.claim: Neil Armstrong was commander; Buzz Aldrin was lunar module pilot; Michael Collins was command module pilot.
facts.evidenceExcerpt:
Neil Armstrong, Commander
Edwin E. “Buzz” Aldrin Jr., Lunar Module Pilot
Michael Collins, Command Module Pilot

facts.claim: Eagle undocked from Columbia on July 20 at 100 hours, 12 minutes into the flight, as reported in NASA's overview.
facts.locator: Mission Highlights, paragraph beginning On July 20
facts.evidenceExcerpt: at 100 hours, 12 minutes into the flight, the Eagle undocked and separated from Columbia for visual inspection

facts.claim: Surface objectives included a television camera, a solar wind composition experiment, a seismic experiment package, a laser-ranging retroreflector and samples returned to Earth.
facts.evidenceExcerpt: deployment of a solar wind composition experiment, seismic experiment package and a Laser Ranging Retroreflector

facts.claim: A commemorative plaque was attached to Eagle's descent stage.
facts.evidenceExcerpt: Attached to the descent stage was a commemorative plaque signed by President Richard M. Nixon and the three astronauts.

facts.claim: A silicon disk carrying miniaturized goodwill messages from 73 countries was left on the Moon.
facts.evidenceExcerpt: A one-and-a-half inch silicon disk, containing micro miniaturized goodwill messages from 73 countries, and the names of congressional and NASA leaders, also stayed behind.

facts.claim: The ascent stage returned to lunar orbit, docked with Columbia, and was later jettisoned after Armstrong and Aldrin returned to the command and service module.
facts.locator: Mission Highlights, paragraph beginning Armstrong and Aldrin spent
facts.evidenceExcerpt: Armstrong and Aldrin returned to the CSM with Collins. Four hours later, the LM jettisoned and remained in lunar orbit.
facts.qualification: Historical sequence only; this is not evidence of its present orbit or final impact location.

facts.claim: The Apollo 11 reflector array has 100 quartz-glass corner cubes and requires no power.
facts.evidenceExcerpt: The Apollo 11 and 14 arrays have 100 quartz glass prisms (called corner cubes) each
facts.additionalEvidenceExcerpt: The arrays themselves require no power.

facts.claim: Lunar laser ranging measures the travel time of laser pulses and has helped determine lunar motion and provided evidence of a fluid lunar core.
facts.locator: Laser timing, lunar motion and core paragraphs
facts.evidenceExcerpt: Analysis of lunar laser data shows that the Moon has a fluid core.
facts.qualification: Findings from the lunar laser-ranging program; do not attribute the whole result exclusively to Apollo 11's array. Article dated 2019, not a live status feed.

facts.claim: NASA Photojournal PIA12909 presents a later LRO narrow-angle-camera view of the Apollo 11 landing site.
facts.evidenceExcerpt: LRO passed over the site again providing LROC a new view of the historic site.
facts.qualification: The source lists September 29, 2009 as Image Addition Date. It is not recorded here as the exposure date.
